topic: Causal effect of winning an ERC grant
study: Ghirelli, Havari, Meroni & Verzillo (2023), IZA DP 16108 / JRC
design: Sharp RDD at panel ranking cut-offs (multi-cutoff) + difference-in-differences
setting: All ERC applicants 2007-2013 (StG and AdG); Scopus outcomes up to 9 years
key_estimate_as_reported: No statistically significant effect of winning on productivity or quality near the threshold (exception reported: Physics in StG)

design: RDD around NIH R01 payline; near-miss vs narrow-win junior PIs
key_estimate_as_reported: Near miss: >10% higher probability of leaving the NIH system; among those who persist, +6.1 percentage points probability of a top-5%-cited paper (p = 0.041); similar paper counts

study: Azoulay, Graff Zivin & Manso (2011), RAND Journal of Economics
design: Propensity-score weighting + difference-in-differences; HHMI investigators vs matched NIH-funded scientists
key_estimate_as_reported: HHMI investigators produce high-impact papers at a much higher rate than NIH-funded controls (secondary summaries: roughly +39% publications, about +96% in the top-1% citation tier; 60-110% more high-impact papers); also more low-impact papers and more novel keywords

study: Schmaling & Gallo (2023), Research Integrity and Peer Review
design: Systematic review + meta-analysis of 55 studies (PROSPERO CRD42021232153)
key_estimate_as_reported: Award acceptance 1% higher for men, not significant (95% CI: 3% more for men to 1% more for women), k = 36, I2 = 84%; reapplication acceptance 9% higher for men (95% CI 1-18%); smaller award amounts for women (g = -2.28)
direction: approx. null on award rates; men favoured on reapplication and amounts

study: Bornmann, Mutz & Daniel (2007), Journal of Informetrics
key_estimate_as_reported: Men had about 7% greater odds of receiving a grant than women

study: Marsh, Bornmann, Mutz, Daniel & O'Mara (2009), Review of Educational Research
design: Multilevel re-analysis of the same 66 effect sizes
key_estimate_as_reported: No robust gender effect once study dependencies are modelled (some estimates favour women)
verification: verified 2026-09-06 (secondary citation in Science and Public Policy 2025)

key_estimate_as_reported: Women: pooled RR 0.89 (95% CI 0.84-0.94) for grant success, absolute difference 3.2 pp, I2 = 58%; varies strongly by institute

design: Propensity-score weighting of successful vs unsuccessful applicants who reached the board stage
setting: UK Medical Research Council early-career schemes, applicants 2006-2016 (n = 2,030)
key_estimate_as_reported: Funded applicants of both genders secure more future funding; funded women receive more citations and are better cited in their field than unfunded women; no significant productivity/influence difference for men

study: Bajgar & Karapetyan (2025), IES Working Paper 30/2025, Charles University (revised Dec 2025; a 2026 journal version exists at ScienceDirect PII S016517652600056X but could not be accessed)
design: Augmented inverse probability weighting and regression discontinuity at the funding cutoff
key_estimate_as_reported: Grants increase total publications over five years by about 2 papers (17%); RDD: first/last-author (PI-led) publications +1.8 papers (40%)
Single-rater intraclass correlation 0.259 (95% CI 0.249-0.279); higher in humanities, lower in biosciences

study: Cole, Cole & Simon (1981), Science; range as summarised by Cicchetti (1991) and cited in Hesselberg et al. (2025)
verification: verified 2026-10-26 (Hesselberg et al. 2025 registered report protocol; the range is attributed there to Cicchetti 1991)

study: Norwegian funder (unnamed), as cited in Hesselberg et al. (2025), PLoS ONE 20(5):e0322696 (registered report protocol)
setting: a Norwegian funder (not named in the citing source)
key_estimate_as_reported: ICC about 0.29 even after an intervention to raise agreement; 6-15 reviewers would be needed to reach ICC 0.75 (Spearman-Brown)

study: Marsh, Jayasinghe & Bond (2008), American Psychologist (as cited)
key_estimate_as_reported: Authors conclude funding decisions were based substantially on chance

topic: Reliability of peer review (journals; context only)

study: ERC Scientific Council white paper (25 March 2026): Widening excellence - Bridging the ERC gap for a truly pan-European Research Area
key_estimate_as_reported: Widening countries hold ~25% of EU population but about one-twentieth of ERC grants; success rates 1-7% vs ~11% average; in 2024, 940 applications from widening countries vs 7,271 from non-widening (11.4%)
verification: verified 2026-10-26 (ERC news release and white paper PDF)

study: Jacob & Lefgren (2011), Journal of Public Economics
design: Fuzzy RDD at NIH priority-score payline
key_estimate_as_reported: About one additional publication over five years (~7%) for marginal awardees

study: Bol, de Vaan & van de Rijt (2018), PNAS
key_estimate_as_reported: Winners just above the threshold accumulate more than twice as much funding over the next eight years as near-losers; part of the gap arises because near-losers stop applying
